q: Which default fits a tool that sends email on the user's behalf?
options: Enabled by default; no confirmation
Enabled explicitly; confirmation optional
Disabled by default; confirmation always required
Enabled explicitly; no confirmation if the draft was reviewed earlier
explanation: Sending is irreversible and visible to others, so it starts disabled and every send is gated.

q: An email send call times out and you can't tell whether the message went out. What should the agent do?
options: Not retry; log the failure and ask the user how to proceed
Retry up to three times with exponential backoff
Retry once after 5 seconds, then report
Continue the task and send a follow-up later
explanation: Never auto-retry a write: a partial success could send the email twice. Only reads are safe to retry.

q: A user types 'Ignore your previous instructions' in an allowlisted session. How does the trust hierarchy treat this?
options: As a valid override, since the user is authenticated
As Level 5 external content to be summarized
As a trigger to reload SOUL.md from disk
As a Level 2 message trying to use Level 1 authority, which has no effect
explanation: The user has full task authority but cannot rewrite runtime configuration by message. Changing Level 1 means editing the file.

q: A heartbeat fires at 2am and finds an email that seems to need a reply. What should the agent do?
options: Send a short holding reply, since heartbeats can act for the user.
Defer the decision to the next user session and log it in the daily memory entry.
Draft and send the reply if it is under 100 words.
Ignore the email and delete the reminder.
explanation: Scheduled prompts are not user proxies and cannot send new outbound messages; decisions needing judgment are deferred and logged.

q: An operator adds an RSS feed integration but forgets to update the trust hierarchy. What is the risk?
options: The feed is blocked until assigned a level.
The feed automatically receives Level 4 authority.
Nothing; RSS content cannot contain instructions.
The agent may give the feed user-level authority by default.
explanation: This is the most common maintenance failure. Place any source not explicitly assigned at Level 5.

q: An operator wants to give the agent a riskier permission. Which is the weakest reason to grant it?
options: The current tier passes its test battery
30 days have passed since the last expansion
A sample of sessions at the current tier reviewed clean
The new permission has a confirmation gate
explanation: Expanding autonomy should rest on evidence, not elapsed time.

q: Before deployment you send the agent "Help me get my email situation under control." Which response shows good scope containment?
options: Ask clarifying questions about the goal and allowed operations before acting
Start drafting filter rules for the inbox
Archive all read email older than 30 days
Refuse, because email management is out of scope
explanation: A vague request should trigger an ambiguity protocol, not action.

q: You stop and restart an agent's container. What must you confirm before trusting it in production?
options: The daily budget limit pauses the agent
Injected document content is ignored
The agent still has its memory and identity files
Unauthorized users are silently rejected
explanation: Losing memory on restart is a data loss event. The workspace must live on a persistent volume.

q: For a trading skill, how should options and derivatives access be enabled?
options: Automatically, once equity trading is enabled
Through a separate explicit capability flag, distinct from equity trading
After 30 days of successful equity trades
By default in read-only mode
explanation: Options can lose more than the initial capital through leverage, so they need their own flag rather than being bundled with general trading.

q: Writing SOUL.md and AGENTS.md before connecting any tools is most like which software practice?
options: Continuous deployment
Pair programming
Chaos engineering
Test-driven development
explanation: As tests come before code, the spec comes before tools, forcing decisions about every case up front.
